headline: The Bank of England just raised rates for the first time since 2023, a day after the Democratic sweep sent the Dow up 1,569 points and oil down 8%.
dateline: Thursday, November 5, 2026 · closes as of Wed Nov 4

rundown.h: Treasury holds coupon auctions steady and signals no change ahead.
rundown.p: Wednesday's quarterly refunding kept nominal coupon sizes flat for a $125 billion package: a $58 billion 3-year on Monday, $42 billion 10-year Tuesday and $25 billion 30-year Thursday. Treasury expects to keep coupon sizes unchanged "for the next several quarters," and set buybacks of up to $95 billion. No surprise supply means one less source of pressure on long-term borrowing costs.

rundown.h: Six Fed speakers get two days to frame December.
rundown.p: Cleveland's Beth Hammack, who dissented in favor of a hike at the Oct. 28 meeting along with Lisa Cook, speaks today with Richmond's Tom Barkin. Friday brings Lorie Logan, John Williams, Alberto Musalem and Michelle Bowman, right after the October jobs report. With the statement saying inflation "remains elevated," any pushback on a December hike would be news.
rundown.src: Federal Reserve; Trading Economics calendar · Nov 5

rundown.h: Election rally rotates money away from AI chips.
rundown.p: Wednesday's rally skipped the AI chip trade: Nvidia fell 3.2% and Micron 7.0% even as Microsoft rose 6.8% and Amazon 6.1%. Nasdaq 100 futures were down about 0.8% early Thursday on fears that a Democratic Congress tightens rules on data centers, a risk worth watching for the power and land buyers chasing that build-out.

rundown.h: AppLovin soars after hours; Qualcomm sinks despite a beat.
rundown.p: AppLovin's third-quarter revenue rose 55% to $2.18 billion, above its own $2.055 to $2.085 billion guidance, net income climbed 72% to $1.44 billion and it spent $1.4 billion on stock; shares jumped about 20% late Wednesday. Qualcomm fell more than 7% after hours even though results topped estimates. ConocoPhillips, Airbnb and Kimberly-Clark report today.

rundown.h: Treasury goes after fake ship registries moving Iranian oil.
rundown.p: OFAC sanctioned 14 people and companies, mostly India-based, that it says ran sham flag registries and certification services claiming to act for countries such as Guyana, Mali and Timor-Leste, which never authorized them. Falsely flagged tankers lack valid P&I insurance, Treasury warned, and could cause billions in damage. Expect more scrutiny, and costs, for anyone chartering, insuring or financing shadow-fleet tonnage.

dive.title: The overnight market is getting tighter, and floating-rate borrowers pay first
dive.dek: SOFR has drifted above the rate the Fed pays on reserves as Treasury's cash pile swells and the Fed's bill buying sits at zero.
dive.body:
If you borrow at a floating rate, your loan doesn't really start at the Fed. It starts in the overnight repo market, where SOFR is set each morning from about $3 trillion of trades. And that market has been quietly tightening. SOFR printed 3.97% on Nov. 3, up from 3.88% on Oct. 14, while the Fed's target range never moved from 3.75% to 4.00%. It now sits 7 basis points above the 3.90% the Fed pays banks on reserves, and just 3 basis points under the 4.00% rate at the Fed's Standing Repo Facility, the market's effective ceiling.

Two things are draining the pool. Bank reserves fell $74 billion in the week to Oct. 28, to $2.895 trillion, down from $3.04 trillion in early September, as Treasury's cash account swelled past $1.0 trillion. Meanwhile the Fed has stopped topping up reserves: it bought about $40 billion a month of bills for "reserve management" early this year, cut to $25 billion and then $10 billion, and has bought none since mid-August. The current schedule, through Nov. 13, again has zero.

Why it matters: a floating-rate loan pays SOFR plus a spread, so a few basis points of repo pressure land straight on construction loans, bridge debt, warehouse lines and the debt funds and mortgage REITs that finance themselves in repo, before the Fed lifts a finger. Interest-rate caps and debt-service coverage tests feel it at the margin. For now this is a squeeze, not a seizure: banks borrowed just $5 million from the repo facility on Nov. 3, and SOFR is well below the 4.22% it hit at the end of October 2025.

What would change the picture: Treasury's own plan assumes its cash balance falls to $850 billion by year-end, which would hand roughly $165 billion back to the banking system. But it then expects to rebuild cash to $1.0 trillion by the end of March while borrowing $800 billion that quarter. Restarting reserve purchases would ease the strain, but with futures leaning toward a December hike, that move would look like easing at an awkward moment.

items.title: October ISM services slipped to 54.5 as orders cooled, but prices paid stayed at 73.0

chart.src: Source: ISM Services PMI report, October 2026 (PR Newswire, Nov 4, 2026).

items.body:
The ISM services index slipped to 54.5 in October from 54.9, a touch under the 54.8 consensus and still in expansion for a services sector that is most of the economy. Its 12-month average is 54.3, with a range of 52.4 to 56.1 over the past year.

The cooling came from demand. Business activity fell to 53.8 from 56.5 and new orders to 55.9 from 59.8. Employment rose to 51.4 from 50.1, above 50 for a second month; backlogs rose to 58.0 and supplier deliveries slowed to 56.7.

Prices paid eased to 73.0 from 74.0, below a 75.0 forecast but above 70 for the seventh time in eight months. Its 12-month average rose to 69.2, the highest since April 2023, and prices have risen 113 months in a row. ISM said tariffs and fuel costs were respondents' most-cited supply-chain issues. On a day dominated by election results, the 2-year Treasury yield closed at 4.58% from 4.61% and the 10-year at 4.90% from 4.95%.

experts.who: Steve Miller, chair, ISM Services Business Survey Committee
experts.view: Said many companies have not yet fully passed fuel and tariff costs on to customers and expect more price pressure unless oil and trade conditions normalize.

experts.who: Adam Button, chief currency analyst, investingLive
experts.view: Read the report as a step back from September showing no big acceleration in the economy, though services remain strong and prices paid are very high.
Argued the headline dip doesn't signal a weakening economy, pointing to the highest backlogs since 2022 and firmer hiring, in a higher-inflation, resilient-growth picture.

items.lean: Analysts quoted read it as cooler demand but sticky prices; economists polled by Reuters expect a December hike.
items.src: Sources: ISM via PR Newswire; Trading Economics; Verified Investing (component forecasts); Reuters via WIKY; investingLive; XTB; U.S. Treasury yields (Nov 4, 2026).

lead.title: The Bank of England hikes for the first time since 2023, and hints it may not be done
lead.body:
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate a quarter point to 4.00% at noon London time today, its first increase since August 2023. The vote was 8–1, with Catherine Mann wanting a bigger half-point move to 4.25%; at the September meeting the committee had held at 3.75% on a 6–3 split. The MPC said activity data had come in stronger than expected and that policy is not on a pre-set path.

The trigger is energy. UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August and 2.9% in July, driven mainly by fuel prices tied to the Middle East conflict, and the Bank now sees inflation peaking near 5% by mid-2027.
lead.reach: Through global bond yields and the dollar: the UK 10-year gilt held near 5.15% after the decision and sterling sat around $1.348, a one-month high (Nov 5), with markets pricing three more UK hikes by November 2027.

views.who: Andrew Bailey, Governor, Bank of England
views.view: Signaled that further rate increases may be needed to bring inflation back to target.
Most expected today's hike, but only about half saw another rise in early 2027, making them more cautious than market pricing.

reading.title: When the mirror talks back
reading.dek: George Soros built a fortune on one uncomfortable idea: market prices don't just reflect reality, they help create it.
reading.body:
Most market theories start from a tidy assumption: prices are a mirror. Fundamentals change, prices reflect them, and the mirror never talks back. George Soros, born in Budapest in 1930 and a student of philosopher Karl Popper at the London School of Economics, thought the mirror was a lot chattier than that. His name for the back-and-forth was reflexivity, an idea he sketched in the early 1960s and laid out publicly in The Alchemy of Finance in 1987.

The core claim is simple. Investors act on their beliefs, and those beliefs are always partly wrong. But their actions move prices, and prices can change the very fundamentals they are supposed to be measuring. A classic example is lending. When property values rise, banks happily lend more against them; the extra credit pushes prices higher, which makes the collateral look even safer, which justifies more lending. Run the movie backward and the same loop drives a collapse.

That loop is the engine of the Soros boom-bust sequence. A trend and a popular belief start reinforcing each other. For a while the story looks confirmed by the data, partly because the story is creating the data. Eventually the gap between perception and reality gets too wide to paper over, sentiment flips, and the unwind tends to be faster and uglier than the run-up. Equilibrium, in this view, is the exception; disequilibrium is the normal weather.

The practical twist is fallibility, which Soros applied to himself first. If everyone's map of the market is flawed, the edge goes to whoever spots the flaw in their own map soonest. He has credited his success less to being right than to recognizing when he wasn't. That mindset didn't make him timid. On Black Wednesday, September 16, 1992, his fund had sold short more than $10 billion of sterling; when Britain crashed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, the profit was estimated at over $1 billion, and the "man who broke the Bank of England" nickname stuck. He saw a policy promise markets had stopped believing, and leaned on it hard.

The lesson isn't "bet the farm." It's to ask, of any hot trade, whether the price is reflecting reality or manufacturing it, and to know in advance what evidence would tell you your thesis was just a story you told yourself. Soros's real superpower was treating his own conviction as a hypothesis, not a fact.

quote.text: I'm only rich because I know when I'm wrong.
quote.src: George Soros, as cited on Wikipedia
